level-1.title: Building your first budget

story.title: The pot of flour
text: A man was given a pot of flour - enough to matter, not enough to change his life. He hung it from a hook above his bed and lay down beneath it.

Lying there, he built the future out loud. He would sell the flour and buy a goat. The goat would have kids, and the kids would be sold for a cow. The cow would give milk to sell, and the milk money would buy more cows.
By the end of the daydream he owned a herd, a house and a full store-room, and he was so pleased with himself that he kicked out his legs.
His foot caught the pot. It came off the hook and broke on the floor, and every step of the plan went with it.
story.moral: Nothing in his plan was impossible. The mistake was counting each step as done before it was. A budget is written from money you actually have, not money the plan says you will have.

summary: A budget has two sides. Money in, and money out.
Money in is called income. Pocket money is income.
Money out is called expenses. Snacks and bus fare are expenses.
Income minus expenses is what you have left.
If the answer is below zero, your plan does not work. Change it before you spend.

questions.prompt: You get ₹300 pocket money and earn ₹50 more helping a neighbour. Your expenses are ₹280. What is left?

image.alt: Two sources of income beside a list of expenses

questions.hint: Add both sources of income first, then subtract expenses.

questions.prompt: Income is ₹300. Expenses are ₹340. What must change for the budget to work?

image.alt: A budget sheet showing expenses higher than income

options.label: Income must double
Expenses must drop by at least ₹40, or income must rise by ₹40
Nothing, ₹40 short is fine

questions.hint: Find exactly how far below zero the plan is before deciding the fix.

questions.scenario: Riya receives ₹500 this week. Her plan is ₹200 for travel, ₹150 for lunch, ₹100 for savings and ₹50 for snacks. She then remembers a required ₹50 workbook.
questions.prompt: How can Riya include the workbook without spending more than ₹500?

options.label: Keep everything and add ₹50 for the workbook
options.consequence: The plan now costs ₹550. The extra ₹50 has no source.

options.label: Use the ₹50 snack money for the workbook
options.consequence: The total stays ₹500. Travel, lunch and the savings goal remain covered.

options.label: Put ₹150 for travel in the budget, though the fare is still ₹200
options.consequence: The sheet adds up, but Riya is ₹50 short when she needs to travel.

questions.hint: A new cost needs money from somewhere. Look for a purchase that can wait.

reasoning.prompt: Why does moving the snack money solve the problem?

options.label: Putting something in a budget makes it cost less.
Savings must never change, even during an emergency.
It gives the same ₹50 a new job instead of counting it twice.

reasoning.hint: Follow the ₹50 from the old plan to the new one.
reasoning.explanation: Adding an expense does not add income. Here, moving the snack money covers the new cost while preserving the existing school needs and saving goal.

level-2.title: Budgeting with the 50-30-20 plan

story.title: The pot of flour
text: A man received a pot of flour, hung it above his sleeping place, and lay down under it to think.

What followed was a chain of entirely reasonable steps. Sell the flour, buy a goat. Breed the goat, sell the kids, buy a cow. Sell the milk, buy more cows. Each link was plausible on its own, and he treated the whole chain as though it had already happened.
Deep in the last step of the daydream he kicked out - and brought the pot down on the floor.
He was left with the same thing he had started with, minus the flour.
story.moral: Every step depended on the one before it succeeding, and he had priced the whole chain at certainty. A budget separates two columns for exactly this reason: money in that has arrived, and money in that is expected. Only the first column can be spent.

summary: The 50-30-20 plan splits income into three parts.
Half goes to needs. Three tenths goes to wants. Two tenths goes to savings.
With ₹1000 income that is ₹500 needs, ₹300 wants, and ₹200 savings.
Track what you actually spend for one month. Compare it to your plan.
Adjust the plan to fit your life. The split is a guide, not a rule.

questions.prompt: Using the 50-30-20 plan, how much of a ₹1500 monthly income goes to wants?

image.alt: A circle split into three parts, with fifteen hundred rupees

questions.hint: Wants get 30 percent. Find 30 percent of 1500.

questions.prompt: Your 50-30-20 plan says ₹200 should go to savings out of ₹1000. After tracking a real month, you only saved ₹80. What does the lesson suggest you should now do?

image.alt: A tracking sheet showing a gap between plan and reality

options.label: Increase the wants percentage instead
Ignore it, tracking does not matter
Compare where the extra ₹120 actually went, and adjust either spending or the plan

questions.hint: Tracking exists to catch exactly this kind of gap between plan and reality.

questions.scenario: For this exercise, a household has ₹10,000 this month. Its essential costs cannot be reduced below ₹6,500 right now. It wants to set aside ₹1,000 for an upcoming school cost. A sample 50-30-20 plan suggests ₹5,000 needs, ₹3,000 wants and ₹2,000 savings.
questions.prompt: Which budget fits this household’s actual needs this month?

options.label: Use the sample split exactly
options.consequence: Only ₹5,000 is assigned to essentials that cost ₹6,500, leaving a ₹1,500 gap.

options.label: Budget ₹6,500 needs, ₹3,000 wants and ₹1,000 savings
options.consequence: The goals are named, but the plan totals ₹10,500 against ₹10,000 income.

options.label: Budget ₹6,500 needs, ₹2,500 wants and ₹1,000 savings
options.consequence: All ₹10,000 has a job, essentials are covered and the planned school saving is included.

questions.hint: First cover actual essentials and the stated school goal. Then find what remains.

options.label: They are a starting guide; a usable budget must fit real costs and income.
Needs must always be 65% of every household’s income.
A budget is only valid when wants exceed savings.

reasoning.hint: A guide cannot make actual bills smaller.
reasoning.explanation: The revised plan meets the facts given here. Different households need different splits, and the plan should be reviewed when income or costs change.

level-3.title: Budgeting when income changes
summary: Many families do not earn the same amount every month. Farming, shop work and gig work rise and fall.
With changing income, build the budget on your lowest normal month, not your best one.
In a good month, put the extra into a buffer. In a thin month, the buffer fills the gap.
Zero-based budgeting gives every rupee a job before the month starts - needs, savings, wants - until nothing is left unplanned.
Yearly costs, like school fees or festivals, should be split into monthly set-asides so they never arrive as a shock.
Each month, compare the plan with what really happened. The difference between them is where you learn.

questions.prompt: A tailor earns ₹9,000 in a slow month and up to ₹15,000 in a busy one. Which income should the monthly budget be built on?

image.alt: A calendar with income going up and down month to month

options.label: ₹15,000, the best month
₹12,000, the average
₹9,000, the lowest normal month

questions.hint: Which number can the family still count on in a bad month?

questions.prompt: You are using zero-based budgeting. You have ₹4,000 and have planned ₹3,600 for needs, savings and wants. What must you do?

image.alt: A budget list with some money not yet given a job

options.label: Give the last ₹400 a job too, like savings or a buffer
Nothing - ₹400 left unplanned is fine
Spend the ₹400 at once so it is not wasted

questions.hint: In this method, every rupee is planned before the month starts.

questions.scenario: A family usually earns between ₹8,000 and ₹12,000 a month. Essentials cost ₹7,000. A known yearly school cost needs ₹500 set aside each month. This month’s income is ₹12,000 and there is no buffer yet.
questions.prompt: Which plan uses this good month to prepare for a lower-income month?

options.label: Commit to spending ₹12,000 every month
options.consequence: The plan works this month, but could exceed a normal ₹8,000 month by ₹4,000.

options.label: Plan regular spending and saving within ₹8,000; put this month’s extra ₹4,000 into a buffer
options.consequence: ₹7,000 essentials and ₹500 school savings fit within the base plan. The extra builds protection for lean months.

options.label: Put all ₹5,000 above essentials into flexible spending
options.consequence: Nothing goes to the school saving goal or the buffer, despite this being a good month.

questions.hint: Decide which amount can support recurring commitments in a normal low month.

reasoning.prompt: Why avoid building recurring spending around ₹12,000?

options.label: This month’s income is the best amount to promise for every future month.
Covering this month’s essentials means the extra has no future job.
A good month is not guaranteed every month; the buffer helps cover future gaps.

reasoning.hint: Separate reliable commitments from income that changes.
reasoning.explanation: An ₹8,000 base allows ₹7,000 essentials, ₹500 school savings and ₹500 for other priorities. The ₹4,000 extra becomes a buffer, not a promise of higher income next month.
